script.title: Daily Life at Manzanar Did Not Mean Freedom
script.description: Schools, worship and daily routines existed inside confinement. This account distinguishes departure photographs from forced arrival.

scenes.narration: Manzanar was not an ordinary town: its residents lived inside a wartime camp surrounded by guarded boundaries.
Families were assigned barracks rooms and shared toilets, showers, and mess halls, with little privacy inside the camp.

diagram.title: Shared facilities
diagram.note: Confinement shaped daily life and privacy.

scenes.narration: Winter temperatures could fall below freezing, while wind carried dust and sand through the Owens Valley camp.
Residents nevertheless organized religious services and community routines, building parts of daily life within imposed restrictions.
Ansel Adams also photographed people loading baggage before leaving Manzanar for relocation during the war.
The elevated view records rows of barracks, part of the landscape where thousands of Japanese Americans were confined.
Schools and community activities did not erase confinement; ordinary routines existed alongside the loss of basic freedom.

diagram.title: Routines within confinement
diagram.note: Daily routines did not make the incarceration voluntary.

sources.title: Reviewed primary-source evidence
sources.content: Executive Order 9066 was issued by Franklin Roosevelt on February 19, 1942. It authorized exclusion from military areas and was followed by forced removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans, many of them American citizens. Families lost liberty, homes and property. In 1988 the Civil Liberties Act acknowledged the injustice, apologized and provided partial restitution to eligible surviving people who had been incarcerated.

sources.title: Reviewed primary-source evidence
sources.content: About two-thirds of people incarcerated at Manzanar were American citizens by birth. Families had days to settle their affairs and could take only what they carried. Manzanar housing was surrounded by barbed wire and guard towers. Barracks had little privacy; toilets, showers and mess halls were shared. Winter could be below freezing; summer heat and wind brought dust and sand. Residents established religious services, schools and community activities. Thousands were confined there. Activities did not remove the fact of confinement.
